datasets.title: Cuba: Copernicus Vegetation Index Anomaly (FAPAR Anomaly)
datasets.description: Fraction of Absorbed Photosynthetically Active Radiation (FAPAR) is a biophysical dimensionless quantity (its values range from 0/no absorption to 1/total absorption) used to assess the greenness and health of vegetation. FAPAR anomalies can be used as an indicator to detect and monitor the impacts of agricultural drought on the growth and productivity of vegetation. The data is presented in 10-day time composite of the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS).. [Source: This metadata record was automatically extracted from the Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX); Original dataset: https://data.humdata.org/dataset/cub-anomalies-fapar-viirs]
datasets.details: Variations in the vegetation health and/or cover could be related to stress factors not related to droughts (e.g., plant diseases, pests, hail, flooding). To determine if changes in FAPAR are linked with a drought event or not, FAPAR data should be interpreted jointly with other indicators (as in the EDO Combined Drought Indicator).

lineage.description: FAPAR values are derived from VIIRS satellite imagery composited over 10-day intervals, with anomalies calculated at each grid cell as deviations from a long-term mean baseline spanning 2012 to the most recent complete year. The resulting raster time series serves as an indicator of agricultural drought stress on vegetation growth and productivity in Cuba.

sources.name: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (JRC)
sources.description: JRC provides the FAPAR anomaly methodology and derived raster products, calculating deviations from a long-term baseline (2012 to present) at each grid cell using VIIRS satellite imagery composited over 10-day intervals.

sources.name: Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS)
sources.description: VIIRS is the satellite sensor providing the raw spectral observations used to compute FAPAR values, which are then composited into 10-day intervals for anomaly calculation.
